title: Design: multi-tenant SaaS, platform SDK, trip tracking
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Multi-tenant isolation models and row level security, versioning and deprecating a platform SDK, and designing a trip management and tracking service with ingestion estimates and state correctness.
source: AWS SaaS Lens; PostgreSQL docs (row security policies, ddl-rowsecurity); Semantic Versioning 2.0.0; Oracle Java docs (@Deprecated); Designing Data-Intensive Applications

questions.prompt: A B2B SaaS has 20,000 small tenants with similar needs and a handful of large ones with compliance demands. Which isolation strategy is the sensible default?

options.text: Pooled tables for the tail, dedicated databases for large tenants
options.why: Right: cheap for the long tail, isolation where contracts demand it.

options.text: A separate database server provisioned for each of the 20,000 tenants
options.why: It is operationally and financially unsustainable at that count.

options.text: One schema per tenant for all 20,000, migrated by hand
options.why: Migrations across tens of thousands of schemas are slow and error-prone.

options.text: A single table without tenant ids, filtered in the UI

questions.explanation: The hybrid (pool plus silo) pattern is the typical answer: shared by default, dedicated by exception.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, turn on row level security for table orders and add a policy named tenant_isolation that only lets rows through where tenant_id equals the uuid in the session setting app.tenant_id.
questions.explanation: The application runs SET app.tenant_id = ... (or set_config) per request or transaction. The table owner and superusers bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is used, so connect as a normal role.

questions.prompt: With schema-per-tenant, 5,000 tenants each have 120 tables. How many tables does the database catalogue hold?
questions.explanation: 5,000 x 120 = 600,000. Large catalogues slow migrations, backups and planner caches, which is why schema-per-tenant is rarely used past a few thousand tenants.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A multi-tenant API needs per-tenant quotas and rate limits.
questions.reason: Shared resources let one tenant's spike exhaust capacity for everyone.

whys.a: Right: the reason is the problem that quotas solve.

questions.explanation: Also isolate with bulkheads: separate pools or queues for large tenants.

questions.prompt: Match each multi-tenant concern to the typical mitigation.

left.text: Customer demands its own encryption keys

right.text: Row level security or a mandatory tenant scope in the data layer
Move that tenant to a dedicated shard using a tenant directory
A per-tenant key in a KMS (envelope encryption)

questions.explanation: Keep a tenant directory (tenant to shard or cell) so moves are a data change, not a code change.

questions.prompt: Your SDK is at version 2.7.3 and you add a new backward-compatible method. What is the minor number of the next release version?
questions.explanation: Semantic Versioning: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features (reset PATCH to 0), PATCH for compatible fixes. So 2.7.3 becomes 2.8.0.

questions.prompt: Which changes to a published Java SDK are breaking under semantic versioning? Select all that apply.

options.why: Right: callers fail to compile or link.

options.text: Changing a public method's return type
options.why: Right: it breaks source and binary compatibility.

options.text: Adding a required parameter to an existing method
options.why: Right: old call sites no longer match.

options.text: Adding a new overload with extra optional options
options.why: Existing callers keep working, so a minor release is enough.

questions.explanation: Prefer adding overloads and deprecating over changing. Deprecate in a minor release, remove in the next major.

questions.prompt: In a Java SDK class, keep the old method String fetch(String id) working by delegating to the new fetch(String id, Options options) with Options.defaults(), and mark the old one deprecated since "2.8" and scheduled for removal.
questions.explanation: Add a Javadoc @deprecated tag naming the replacement. Python equivalent: warnings.warn(..., DeprecationWarning, stacklevel=2).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A platform SDK should avoid exposing third-party library types in its public API.
questions.reason: Java generics are erased at compile time.

whys.a: Erasure is unrelated to the dependency leak.
whys.b: Right: both are true but unrelated; the real reason is that upgrading the library would become a breaking change for the SDK.

questions.explanation: Wrap external types in your own interfaces and shade or relocate internal dependencies.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A platform SDK should never be released on a schedule different from the services it calls.
questions.reason: Services and clients are deployed at different times, so the wire contract must tolerate version skew.

whys.d: Right: the assertion is false because independent release cycles are normal; the reason is true and is why compatibility rules matter.

questions.explanation: Use additive wire changes, ignore unknown fields and support at least N-1 versions of the API.

questions.prompt: One million trips are in progress and each driver app sends a GPS ping every 5 seconds. How many pings per second must the ingestion path handle on average?
questions.explanation: 1,000,000 / 5 = 200,000 per second. That justifies a partitioned log such as Kafka keyed by trip id rather than direct database writes.

questions.prompt: The ingestion rate is 200,000 pings per second and each stored ping is 50 bytes. How many decimal gigabytes are written per day?
questions.explanation: 200,000 x 50 B = 10 MB/s; times 86,400 s = 864 GB. Keep hot data short and downsample or compress older pings.

questions.prompt: Which pipeline fits live trip tracking with both a "where is the driver now" view and replayable history?

options.text: A log keyed by trip id feeding a latest-position store
options.why: Right: ordered per trip, fast reads of the latest point and cheap history.

options.text: Pings written straight into a single relational row per trip, updated in place
Pings emailed to the dispatcher once every minute
options.why: No real-time view and no replay.

options.text: Only store the final trip route once the whole trip has ended
options.why: Live tracking is impossible and a crash loses the route.

questions.explanation: Key by trip id to keep a trip's pings in order within one partition.

questions.prompt: Complete the correctness notes for the trip service.
questions.text: Guard concurrent trip updates with optimistic {1} on a version column, make retried "end trip" calls safe with an {2} key, and order GPS pings by the device {3} rather than the arrival time.
questions.explanation: Mobile networks reorder and retry messages, so correctness cannot rely on arrival order or on exactly-once delivery.

questions.prompt: Write the SQL that completes a trip: set status to COMPLETED and increment version, but only if the row with id = 7 is still in status STARTED and has version = 3.
questions.model:
UPDATE trips SET status = 'COMPLETED', version = version + 1
WHERE id = 7 AND status = 'STARTED' AND version = 3;
questions.explanation: If zero rows are updated, someone else changed the trip first, so reload or reject. This single statement is the optimistic lock and the state transition guard together.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: The "latest position" lookup is best served from a key-value store keyed by trip id.
questions.reason: Time-series databases are unable to store GPS coordinates.

whys.c: Right: time-series stores hold coordinates fine; the key-value choice is about O(1) latest-value reads.
whys.d: The assertion is the true statement.

questions.explanation: Use a time-series or object store for history and a KV store like Redis for the current point.

questions.prompt: True or false: in PostgreSQL the owner of a table is always subject to its row level security policies once ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY has been run.

options.why: Incorrect: by default the table owner bypasses RLS.
Right: owners (and superusers or roles with BYPASSRLS) skip policies unless the owner opts in with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

questions.explanation: Use a separate non-owner application role without BYPASSRLS, and consider FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. With RLS enabled and no policy, non-owner roles see no rows (default deny).

questions.prompt: True or false: under Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, versions 0.y.z are for initial development and anything may change at any time.

options.why: Right: spec item 4 says the public API should not be considered stable while the major version is zero.
Incorrect: stability promises only begin at 1.0.0; 0.y.z carries no compatibility guarantee.

questions.explanation: Release 1.0.0 when users depend on the API; from then on, breaking changes need a new major version.
